unitTitle: Chemical Bonding and Shapes of Molecules
syllabusTopics: Valence shell, valence electron and octet theory
Covalent bond and coordinate covalent bond; properties of covalent compounds
Lewis dot structure of some common compounds of s and p block elements
VSEPR theory and shapes of simple molecules (BeF2, BF3, CH4, CH3Cl, PCl5, SF6, H2O, NH3, CO2, H2S, PH3)
Elementary idea of Valence Bond Theory
Hybridization involving s and p orbitals only
Bond characteristics: bond length, ionic character, dipole moment
Vander Waal's force and molecular solids; hydrogen bonding and its application
Metallic bonding and properties of metallic solids

rows.label: Formula
rows.text: - Resonance energy = E(best canonical) − E(hybrid) - Bond order (O₃ hybrid) = 1.5; (CO₃²⁻) = 1⅓; (benzene C–C) = 1.5 - FC = V − (N + ½B) — used to rank canonical forms

rows.label: Conditions
rows.text: **↔ is not ⇌:** resonance is not an equilibrium between interconverting structures — there is no flipping, only one hybrid.  ·  **Equal bond lengths are the proof, not a coincidence:** whenever measured bonds sit between single and double values, think resonance — that is the experimental signature.

rows.label: Quick concepts
rows.text: Bond order between 1 and 2 plus equal bond lengths is the experimental fingerprint of resonance — quote the measured pm values to convert a theory answer into an evidence answer.

rows.label: Key points
rows.text: Resonance: single Lewis structure insufficient → two or more canonical forms (electrons move, atoms never) → real molecule is the more stable hybrid. Examples: O₃ (bond order 1.5, 128 pm), CO₃²⁻ (three forms, 1⅓), benzene (two Kekulé, 139 pm, resonance energy ≈150 kJ mol⁻¹), SO₂, NO₃⁻.…

rows.label: Universal facts
rows.text: Ozone's partial positive central oxygen and partial negative terminals make it both a strong oxidant and a dipolar molecule — resonance chemistry with weather-scale consequences (the ozone layer).

rows.text: ## 5. Comparison Tables **Single structure vs resonance hybrid** | Basis | One canonical form | Resonance hybrid | |---|---|---| | Electron positions | Fixed | Delocalised | | Bond lengths | Single and double distinct | All equal, intermediate | | Stability | Lower | Highest (resonance energy gained) | | Reactivity |…  ·  ## 6. Common Confusions **The molecule does not oscillate between forms:** resonance is a static averaging — the hybrid exists all the time; the canonical forms are bookkeeping, never real intermediates.  ·  **Atoms never move in resonance:** only π electrons and lone pairs shift; any "structure" with a relocated H or O is a different molecule (a tautomer), not a resonance form.

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: **More forms ≠ more stability automatically:** quality (octets, charge placement) matters; equivalent forms contribute equally regardless of count.  ·  ## 7.
